points.description: States that the bridge table holds a mapping between stations/destination (MAC) addresses and the outgoing LAN interface/port/link through which they can be reached (a timestamp per entry may also be mentioned).

levels.says: Mentions only addresses or only ports/interfaces without clearly linking them as a mapping.

points.description: Backward learning: table starts empty; on receiving a frame, the bridge records the frame's SOURCE address with the LAN/port it arrived on ("source Q reachable via L"), i.e. it learns by observing incoming traffic; entries are timestamped/updated/aged out. Learning from the destination address is wrong.

levels.says: Says the table is filled by observing incoming frames' source address and arrival port, but gives no mention of the initial empty state, flooding or timestamp/aging.

points.description: Forwarding use: for a frame, look up the destination address; if an entry exists, forward only on that port (selective forwarding; drop if same LAN as source); if unknown, flood on all other ports.
One benefit: reduces unnecessary flooding/duplication, lowers congestion/traffic, or uses bandwidth better than flooding every frame.

rubric.notes: Full marks need: table maps MAC addresses to ports; learned from the source address and arrival port of incoming frames (starting empty, with timestamps for aging); used to forward selectively (flood if unknown); and one benefit such as less flooding or congestion. Part marks for incomplete versions of the first two points. Learning from destination addresses earns nothing for P2. Accept equivalent wording.
